title: How to start your thread in cross-stitch
subtitle: The knot-free methods that keep the back tidy
excerpt: Cross-stitch starts without a knot. Two methods keep the tail secure: the waste-knot method for the first thread on a new piece, and the under-loop method for subsequent threads. Both anchor the tail under the first few stitches so the back stays flat.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, needlework chapter on thread management. Knot-free starting methods are the universal standard in counted cross-stitch; both methods described here appear in Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: The knot-free method of securing the first few centimetres of a new thread in cross-stitch. The tail is anchored under the first stitches worked over it so no knot shows on the back of the fabric. Two main methods are the waste knot and the under-loop start.

A temporary knot placed on the front of the fabric a few centimetres away from the starting hole. The thread passes to the back and the first stitches are worked over the tail, locking it in place. The knot is snipped off once the tail is secured.

content.text: Cross-stitch starts without a knot. A knot on the back creates a bump under the fabric that shows through the finished piece and can make framing uneven. Two methods anchor the thread cleanly: the
waste knot
for the very first thread on a new piece, and the under-loop method for every thread that follows.
Both methods rely on the same principle: the tail is held on the back of the fabric and the first few
cross-stitches
are worked over it, locking it in place without any knot. Once the tail is secured under four to six stitches, it will not come free.
The waste-knot method (first thread on a new piece)
Tie a small knot at the cut end of the thread.
Push the needle down through the front of the fabric about four to five centimetres from where your first stitch will be, so the knot sits on top of the fabric.
Work the first few stitches toward the knot.
The thread on the back runs from the knot toward your working area. Each stitch worked over that thread locks it in place. Work four to six stitches, moving toward the knot.
Snip the knot.
Once the stitches cover the tail, snip the knot from the front. The thread is now locked in place with nothing protruding from the back.
The under-loop method (when existing stitches are nearby)
Thread the needle and leave no knot.
Thread two strands of floss through the needle eye and hold the cut ends. Do not knot them.
Slide the needle under nearby stitches on the back.
Flip the work over. Pass the needle under four to six existing stitches that are close to where you want to start. Pull the thread through, leaving a short tail.
Trim the tail and begin stitching.
Trim any tail that remains on the back to within two to three millimetres of the stitches. The thread is now anchored and you can start stitching from the front.
Which method to use

Use the waste-knot method only for the first thread, when there are no existing stitches to slide under. Use the under-loop method for every subsequent thread once some stitches are already in place. The under-loop is faster and leaves less on the back.
The rule for
starting thread
in cross-stitch is always the same: secure the tail without a knot, keep the back flat.
